title: SAML
summary: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based standard for exchanging authentication and authorisation assertions between an identity provider and a service provider, and it remains the dominant federation protocol in enterprise and government environments. In the common web browser profile, an unauthenticated user is redirected to the identity provider, authenticates there, and is returned to the service provider carrying a signed assertion posted to an assertion consumer service endpoint. The service provider must validate the XML signature over the assertion, confirm the audience restriction matches its own entity identifier, verify the NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter conditions and the subject confirmation method, and reject any assertion that is replayed. Those checks are exactly where real breaches have occurred: libraries that parse untrusted XML without disabling external entity resolution, service providers that trust an unsigned assertion because it arrived over TLS, and implementations that accept a signature covering only part of the document while the attacker modifies another part. Signature wrapping, XML external entity injection, comment-field confusion and assertion replay are the recurring failure modes, and they are implementation defects rather than flaws in the protocol. Metadata, certificate rotation and clock skew are the operational problems that cause outages, while attribute mapping and name identifier format issues cause the subtle authorisation errors that let a user reach an application they should not. For defenders, SAML troubleshooting means reading identity provider sign-in logs alongside the service provider's own assertion handling, and treating any change in signing certificate or assertion consumer endpoint as a change worth alerting on.
objectives: You will be able to trace a SAML web browser SSO flow and name the security checks the service provider must perform on every assertion.
You will be able to explain signature wrapping, assertion replay and XML external entity risks without relying on a specific tool.
You will be able to inspect SAML metadata, signing certificates and attribute mappings for a federation partnership.
You will be able to diagnose common SAML failures such as clock skew, audience mismatch and unresolved name identifiers.
You will be able to design monitoring for assertion consumer endpoint changes and signing certificate rotation.
You will be able to explain why transmitting an assertion over TLS does not remove the need for signature validation.

beginner.definition: Security Assertion Markup Language, or SAML, is a way for one sign-in service to tell another application that you are who you say. The service sends a signed statement, written in a markup format that labels each field. The application checks the signature before trusting the statement.
beginner.whyItMatters: SAML still runs sign-in for many large organisations. The protocol itself is sound, but the checking code is often weak. Some applications trust a statement just because it arrived over a secure connection. Others check only part of the document. Those small gaps have caused real account takeovers, so careful validation matters.
howItWorks: You open an application, and it sees that you are not signed in yet.
The application sends your browser to the identity provider, the trusted sign-in service.
You sign in there, often with a second factor such as a code or key.
The provider builds a signed statement about you and sends it back.
The application verifies the signature, the audience, and the time limits.
beginner.example: Think of a letter of introduction sealed with wax. A trusted office writes that you are a member of staff and stamps it. You carry the letter to another building. The guard there checks the wax stamp and the name on the envelope. If the stamp is missing, or the letter names a different building, the guard refuses you.
takeaways: A signed SAML statement should be verified, never accepted on transport alone.
Check the audience, the time window, and the full signature.
Alert on changes to signing certificates and receiving endpoints.
